4  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
5       This case arises from Defendants’ alleged scheme to defraud Sage of over $10.8 million 
6  through Defendants’ deceptive acquisition and invocation of a lucrative termination payment 
7  provision in the hospital management agreement between RDC and Sage (the “Management 
8  Services Contract”), followed by Defendants’ billing for services not rendered. (See generally 
9  Compl., ECF No. 1).  Sage is a federally funded non-profit hospital serving an indigent Navajo 
10  Nation community in rural Ganado, Arizona. (Id. ¶ 23).  The majority of Sage’s operation 
11  budget comes from the Indian Health Service (“IHS”), an agency within the U.S. Department 
12  of Health and Human Services. (Id. ¶ 24).  Principally, Sage alleges that Defendants 
13  fraudulently induced Sage’s Board of Directors (“BOD”) to unwittingly authorize a contractual 
14  amendment to the parties’ Management Services Contract containing an extremely generous 
15  termination payment, which Defendants invoked to siphon $10.8 million from Sage’s operating 
16  budget. (See id. ¶¶ 39–57).  The Court’s below discussion provides background on the 
17  relationship between Sage and Defendants, up to and including the scheme described in the 
18  Complaint.

21  Nation and reside in the community in or around Ganado, Arizona. (Id. ¶ 21).  Sometime in 
22  2007, “Razaghi and his brother partnered with a friend, Manuel Morgan (‘Morgan’), a member 

23  of the Navajo Tribe and former Navajo Nation County Commissioner, to form Morgan & 
24  Associates, LLC, a company in which Morgan [held] majority ownership so that the entity 
25  could qualify as a Navajo business.” (Id. ¶ 26).  Sage alleges that Razaghi, leveraging Morgan’s 
1  status as a member of the Navajo Nation, persuaded Sage to award Morgan & Associates a 
2  management services contract. (Id. ¶ 27).  Under the terms of this contract, Razaghi would 
3  serve as Sage’s “Contract CEO.” (Id.).  Sage claims Razaghi subsequently created business 
4  entities, including RDC, to supply Sage with medical personnel at a profit. (Id. ¶ 28).

6  BOD. (Id. ¶ 29).  This contract replaced Morgan & Associates’ contract with the hospital and

8  when the “multiple different schemes to defraud Sage Memorial began through the use of the 
9  mail and interstate wires.” (Id.).

6  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
7       A.   12(b)(1)                                                        
8       Rule 12(b)(1) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure permits motions to dismiss for 
9  lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(1).  When subject matter jurisdiction is 
10  challenged, the burden of proof is placed on the party asserting that jurisdiction exists. Scott v. 
11  Breeland, 792 F.2d 925, 927 (9th Cir. 1986) (holding that “[t]he party seeking to invoke the 
12  court’s jurisdiction bears the burden of establishing that jurisdiction exists”).  Accordingly, the 
13  court will presume lack of subject matter jurisdiction until the plaintiff proves otherwise in 
14  response to the motion to dismiss. Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375, 
15  377 (1994).                                                              
16      A motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) may be construed in one of two ways. 
17  Thornhill Publ’g Co., Inc. v. Gen. Tel. & Elec. Corp., 594 F.2d 730, 733 (9th Cir. 1979).  It 
18  may be described as ‘facial,’ meaning that it attacks the sufficiency of the allegations to support 
19  subject matter jurisdiction. Id.  Alternatively, it may be described as ‘factual,’ meaning that it 
20  “attack[s] the existence of subject matter jurisdiction in fact.” Id.  When, as here, a court 
21  considers a ‘facial’ attack made pursuant to Rule 12(b)(1), it must consider the allegations of 
22  the complaint to be true and construe them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. Love v. 

23  United States, 915 F.2d 1242, 1245 (9th Cir. 1989).

1       B.   12(b)(6)                                                        
2       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) mandates that a court dismiss a cause of action 
3  that fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. See N. Star Int’l v. Ariz. Corp. 
4  Comm’n, 720 F.2d 578, 581 (9th Cir. 1983).  When considering a motion to dismiss under Rule 
5  12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, dismissal is appropriate only when the complaint does not 
6  give the defendant fair notice of a legally cognizable claim and the grounds on which it rests. 
7  See Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007).  In considering whether the 
8  complaint is sufficient to state a claim, the Court will take all material allegations as true and 
9  construe them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. See NL Indus., Inc. v. Kaplan, 792 
10  F.2d 896, 898 (9th Cir. 1986).                                           
11      The Court, however, is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely 
12  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences. See Sprewell v. Golden 
13  State Warriors, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir. 2001).  A formulaic recitation of a cause of action 
14  with conclusory allegations is not sufficient; a plaintiff must plead facts showing that a 
15  violation is plausible, not just possible. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (citing 
16  Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).                                               
17      A court may also dismiss a complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) 
18  for failure to comply with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a). Hearns v. San Bernardino 
19  Police Dept., 530 F.3d 1124, 1129 (9th Cir. 2008).  Rule 8(a)(2) requires that a plaintiff’s 
20  complaint contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled 
21  to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2).  Furthermore, the Supreme Court has rejected any sort of 
22  “heightened” pleading requirement for § 1983 municipal liability claims because such a 

23  heightened pleading standard cannot be “square[d] . . . with the liberal system of ‘notice 
24  pleading’ set up by the Federal Rules.” Leatherman v. Tarrant Cty. Narcotics Intelligence & 
25  Coordination Unit, 507 U.S. 163, 164 (1993).                             
1       “Generally, a district court may not consider any material beyond the pleadings in ruling 
2  on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion . . . . However, material which is properly submitted as part of the 
3  complaint may be considered on a motion to dismiss.” Hal Roach Studios, Inc. v. Richard 
4  Feiner & Co., 896 F.2d 1542, 1555 n.19 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).  Similarly, 
5  “documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party 
6  questions, but which are not physically attached to the pleading, may be considered in ruling on 
7  a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss” without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for 
8  summary judgment. Branch v. Tunnell, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994).  Under Federal Rule 
9  of Evidence 201, a court may take judicial notice of “matters of public record.” Mack v. S. Bay 
10  Beer Distrib., 798 F.2d 1279, 1282 (9th Cir. 1986).  Otherwise, if the district court considers 
11  materials outside of the pleadings, the motion to dismiss becomes a motion for summary 
12  judgment. See Arpin v. Santa Clara Valley Transp. Agency, 261 F.3d 912, 925 (9th Cir. 2001). 
13      Additionally, “[i]n alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity the 
14  circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).  The rule requires that claims 
15  of fraud be accompanied by the “who, what, when, where, and how” of the conduct charged, 
16  Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp., USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1106 (9th Cir. 2003) (quoting Cooper v. 
17  Pickett, 137 F.3d 616, 627 (9th Cir. 1997)), so that the complaint may not simply “lump 
18  multiple defendants together.” Destfino v. Reiswig, 630 F.3d 952, 958 (9th Cir. 2011).  In other 
19  words, the complaint “must include ‘an account of the time, place, and specific content of the 
20  false representations as well as the identities of the parties to the misrepresentations.’” Depot, 
21  Inc. v. Caring for Montanans, Inc., 915 F.3d 643, 668 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Swartz v. 
22  KPMG, LLP, 476 F.3d 756, 764 (9th Cir. 2007) (per curiam)) (internal quotations omitted).  

23  Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement ensures that the defendants are on “notice of the particular 
24  misconduct . . . so that they can defend against the charge and not just deny that they have done 
25  anything wrong.” Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106 (internal quotations omitted).   
1       If the court grants a motion to dismiss, it must then decide whether to grant leave to 
2  amend.  The court should “freely give” leave to amend when there is no “undue delay, bad 
3  faith[,] dilatory motive on the part of the movant . . . undue prejudice to the opposing party by 
4  virtue of . . . the amendment, [or] futility of the amendment . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a); Foman 
5  v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962).  Generally, leave to amend is only denied when it is clear 
6  that the deficiencies of the complaint cannot be cured by amendment. See DeSoto v. Yellow 
7  Freight Sys., Inc., 957 F.2d 655, 658 (9th Cir. 1992).                    
8       C.   Report and Recommendation                                       
9       This Court “may accept, reject, or modify, in whole or in part, the findings or 
10  recommendations made by the magistrate judge.” 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1).  Where a party timely 
11  objects to a magistrate judge’s report and recommendation, then the court is required to “make 
12  a de novo determination of those portions of the [report and recommendation] to which 
13  objection is made.” Id.                                                  
14      D.   Motion to Strike                                                
15      The Court may strike “from a pleading an insufficient defense or any redundant, 
16  immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(f).  “[T]he function of a Rule 
17  12(f) motion to strike is to avoid the expenditure of time and money that must arise from 
18  litigating spurious issues by dispensing with those issues prior to trial. . . .” Sidney–Vinstein v. 
19  A.H. Robins Co., 697 F.2d 880, 885 (9th Cir. 1983).  The decision to grant or deny a motion to

7                   4.  Pattern of Racketeering Activity                     
8       Defendants argue that even if Sage has alleged predicate acts, it has not demonstrated a 
9  pattern of racketeering activity. (MTD 17:17–19:13).  More specifically, Defendants contend 
10  Sage has not alleged continuity between the purported predicate acts of racketeering. (Id.).   
11      A “pattern of racketeering activity” requires “at least two acts of racketeering activity, 
12  one of which occurred after the effective date of this chapter and the last of which occurred 
13  within ten years . . . after the commission of a prior act of racketeering activity.” 18 U.S.C. § 
14  1961(5).  While two predicate racketeering acts, as described in § 1961(1), “are necessary” to 
15  plead a civil RICO claim, “they may not be sufficient.” H.J. Inc. v. Nw. Bell Tel. Co., 492 U.S. 
16  229, 237–38 (1989) (quoting Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., Inc., 473 U.S. 479, 496 n.14 
17  (1985)).  There is more to showing a “pattern” of racketeering activity than “simply [pointing 
18  to] the number of predicate acts involved.” Id. at 238.  A pattern requires that the acts have “the 
19  same or similar purposes, results, participants, victims, or methods of commission, or otherwise 
20  are interrelated by distinguishing characteristics. . . .” Sun Sav. and Loan Ass’n v. Dierdorff, 
21  825 F.3d 187, 192 (9th Cir. 1987) (quoting Sedima, S.P.R.L. v. Imrex Co., 473 U.S. 479 n.14 
22  (1985)).                                                                 

23      A “pattern” of racketeering activity is established by two requisite elements, relatedness 
24  and continuity, where continuity need not be alleged with certainty to overcome a motion to 
25  dismiss. H. J., Inc., 492 U.S. at 239, 250.  The continuity element has two types: closed-ended 
1  and open-ended. Id. at 241.  If either type is plausibly identified by the allegations, continuity is 
2  adequately alleged. Id.  Generally, closed-ended continuity refers to repeated conduct over a 
3  specifically defined period of time; whereas, open-ended continuity refers to the threat of 
4  continued racketeering activity. Id. at 241–42.                           
5       With respect to the alleged pattern, the Court finds that Sage has adequately alleged the 
6  predicate acts are related.  The mailings and wire communications were allegedly executed to 
7  improperly receive funds from Sage pursuant to the fraudulently procured Management 
8  Services Contract.  The Court next considers whether Sage has adequately alleged either 
9  possible theory of continuity between the predicate acts.                 
10                     a.  Closed-Ended Continuity                           
11      A plaintiff may allege closed-ended continuity through a single scheme to defraud “so 
12  long as the predicate acts involved are not isolated or sporadic.” Kearny v. Foley & Lardner, 
13  607 F. App’x 757, 759 (9th Cir. 2015) (quoting Turner v. Cook, 362 F.3d 1219, 1229 (9th Cir. 
14  2004); Sun Sav. and Loan Ass’n, 825 F.2d at 193–94; see also Turner, 362 F.3d at 1230 
15  (“multiple criminal episodes are not required to establish a pattern of racketeering under 
16  RICO.”).  While closed-ended continuity requires that the alleged predicate acts have occurred 
17  over a “substantial period of time,” there is no rigid time requirement for the duration of the 
18  alleged scheme. Allwaste v. Hecht, 65 F.3d 1523, 1528 (9th Cir. 1993) (rejecting a bright line, 
19  one-year rule).                                                          
20      Generally, if alleged conduct only “extend[ed] over a few weeks or months,” the 
21  allegations do not support a theory of closed-ended continuity. H.J. Inc., 492 U.S. at 242.  
22  While the Ninth Circuit has rejected a one-year per se rule, if the alleged conduct occurred over 

23  a period under one year, then a scheme involving a limited number of participants and a limited 
24  number of victims is insufficient to establish closed-ended continuity. See Kan-Di-Ki, LLC v. 
25  Sorenson, 723 F. App’x 432, 434 (9th Cir. 2018)

2  of time.  While the Complaint contends that “the Razaghi-Hasan Enterprise has been ongoing

11  valid contractual relationship, (2) knowledge of the relationship on the part of the interferor, (3) 
12  intentional interference inducing or causing a breach, (4) resultant damage to the party whose 
13  relationship has been disrupted, and (5) that the defendant acted improperly.” Wells Fargo, 38 
14  P.3d at 31.  Arizona courts also recognize a claim for tortious interference where the defendant 
15  has not caused a breach, but has made the plaintiff’s performance “more expensive or 
16  burdensome.” Plattner v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 812 P.2d 1129, 1134 (Ariz. Ct. App.

1  and open-ended. Id. at 241.  If either type is plausibly identified by the allegations, continuity is 
2  adequately alleged. Id.  Generally, closed-ended continuity refers to repeated conduct over a 
3  specifically defined period of time; whereas, open-ended continuity refers to the threat of 
4  continued racketeering activity. Id. at 241–42.

(b)(1)(B).  Parties may then object to “such

3

5                                                                            
        vs.                          )

10       Pending before the Court is the Motion for Preliminary Injunction, (ECF No. 18), filed 
11  by Plaintiff Navajo Health Foundation (“Plaintiff”).  Defendants Razaghi Development 
12  Company, LLC, Ahmad R. Razaghi, and Tausif Hasan (collectively “Defendants”) filed a 
13  Motion to Stay Briefing and Consideration of Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, 
14  (ECF No. 22), or in the alternative, a Motion for Extension of Time to File Response, (ECF No. 
15  23).  For the reasons stated herein, Plaintiff’s Motion is denied, and Defendants’ Motions are 
16  denied as moot.                                                           
17  I.   BACKGROUND                                                           
18       Plaintiff, an Arizona non-profit corporation, administers and operates Sage Memorial 
19  Hospital (the “hospital”), which is located within the territorial boundaries of the Navajo 
20  Nation. (Compl. ¶ 7, ECF No. 1).  In 2018, Defendant Razaghi served as the contract CEO for 
21  the hospital and was the sole and controlling member of Defendant Razaghi Development 
22  Company, LLC (“RDC”), a healthcare management company. (Id. ¶ 9).  Defendant Hasan 
23  served as contract CFO for Sage Memorial and was an employee of RDC. (Id. ¶ 10).  RDC was 
24  under contract to provide management services for the hospital. (Id. ¶ 29).  Plaintiff alleges, 
25  inter alia, that in July 2018, the hospital’s board of directors (the “Board”) began to question its 
   contractual relationship with Defendants. (See id. ¶¶ 49–53).  On August 20, 2018 the Board 
1  convened an executive session meeting and discussed the hospital’s contract with RDC 
2  management and payments made to RDC. (Id. ¶ 54).  At that time, it was decided that the 
3  Board would not be approving an incentive bonus for Razaghi that year. (Id.).  Plaintiff further 
4  alleges that on August 27, 2018, Hasan called the hospital’s finance department seeking the 
5  status of a $10,855,134.15 RDC invoice submitted earlier that day. (Id. ¶ 55).  The subject line 
6  on the invoice merely referenced a “Contract Termination Fee, Section 5.D.” (Id.).  After 
7  Hasan’s phone call, a finance staff member then input the invoice into the hospital’s payment 
8  system and notified Hasan. (Id.).  Hasan then transferred monies from the hospital’s bank 
9  accounts into the hospital’s general operating account to cover the invoice. (Id.).  Minutes 
10  thereafter, Hasan in his capacity as contract CFO, approved the $10,855,134.15 invoice, and 
11  payment was issued to RDC. (Id.).  Plaintiff alleges that the invoice contained 
12  misrepresentations; the $10,855,134.15 transfer was not authorized by the hospital’s Board; and 
13  that Defendants’ actions constitute fraud. (See id. ¶¶ 2, 55, 62)         
14       On February 22, 2019, Plaintiff filed a Complaint, (ECF No. 1), against Defendants 
15  asserting the following causes of action: (1) Declaratory and Injunctive Relief; (2) Federal Civil 
16  RICO; (3) Federal Civil RICO Conspiracy; (4) Nevada Civil RICO; (5) Nevada Civil RICO 
17  Conspiracy; (6) Conversion; (7) Civil Conspiracy; (8) Tortious Interference with Contract; (9) 
18  Common Law Fraud; (10) Constructive Fraud; and (11) Aiding and Abetting.  The parties’ 
19  motions now follow.                                                       
20  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
21       Injunctive relief is “an extraordinary remedy that may only be awarded upon a clear 
22  showing that the plaintiff is entitled to such relief.” Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 
23  7, 22 (2008).  A plaintiff seeking a preliminary injunction must establish four elements: (1) 
24  “that he is likely to succeed on the merits,” (2) “that he is likely to suffer irreparable harm in 
25  the absence of preliminary relief,” (3) “that the balance of equities tips in his favor,” and (4) 
1  “that an injunction is in the public interest.” Id. at 20.  “[C]ourts must balance the competing 
2  claims of injury and must consider the effect on each party of the granting or withholding of the 
3  requested relief.” Id. at 24 (internal quotation marks omitted).          
4        The Ninth Circuit has held that “serious questions going to the merits and a hardship 
5  balance that tips sharply toward the plaintiff can support issuance of an injunction, assuming 
6  the other two elements of the Winter test are also met.” Alliance for the Wild Rockies v. 
7  Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127, 1132 (9th Cir. 2011) (internal quotation marks omitted). 
8  III.  DISCUSSION                                                          
9       Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction seeks what it characterizes as “two very 
10  simple things”: (1) a hearing to ascertain the location of the $10,855,134.15 allegedly taken by 
11  Defendants, and (2) an order directing those funds be placed into a trust account maintained by 
12  a third-party custodian pending the adjudication of this case. (Pl.’s Mot. Prelim. Inj. (“Mot”) at 
13  2, ECF No. 18).  In order to determine whether this “extraordinary remedy” is warranted, 
14  Winter, 555 U.S. at 22, the Court will first address whether Plaintiff’s requested injunction is 
15  prohibitory or mandatory.  The Court will then consider whether Plaintiff has established the 
16  requisite preliminary injunction elements under Winter.                   
17       A.   Plaintiff requests a mandatory preliminary injunction           
18       A preliminary injunction may be either prohibitory or mandatory.  “A prohibitory 
19  injunction prohibits a party from taking action and preserves the status quo pending a 
20  determination of the action on the merits.” Marlyn Nutraceuticals, Inc. v. Mucos Pharma 
21  GmbH & Co., 571 F.3d 873, 878 (9th Cir. 2009) (internal quotations and alterations omitted).  
22  The status quo means “the last, uncontested status which preceded the pending controversy.” 
23  Regents of the Univ. of Cal. v. Am. Broad. Cos., 747 F.2d 511, 514 (9th Cir. 1984).  
24       In contrast, a mandatory injunction “orders a responsible party to ‘take action’” Meghrig 
25  v. KFC W., Inc., 516 U.S. 479, 484 (1996).  Mandatory injunctions are disfavored and “are not 
1  granted unless extreme or very serious damage will result.” Anderson v. United States, 612 
2  F.2d 1112, 1115 (9th Cir. 1980).  They “are not issued in doubtful cases or where the injury 
3  complained of is capable of compensation in damages.” Id.                 
4       Here, Plaintiff’s requested injunction is mandatory because it seeks to compel 
5  Defendants to do something they are not currently doing; that is, deposit funds into a third-
6  party trust account.  Insofar as Plaintiff represents that granting the injunction would return 
7  Plaintiff to the status quo prior to Defendants’ allegedly wrongful taking of $10.8 million, 
8  Plaintiff is mistaken. (Mot. at 11).  The status quo means “the last, uncontested status which 
9  preceded the pending controversy.’” Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 747 F.2d at 514.  And the 
10  “last uncontested status” is not measured from the time at which the first dispute at issue in a 
11  case arose, but from the time the complaint was filed. See N.D. ex rel. parents acting as 
12  guardians ad litem v. Hawaii Dep’t of Educ., 600 F.3d 1104, 1112 n.6 (9th Cir. 2010) 
13  (preliminary injunction prohibiting enforcement of new furlough policy was “prohibitory” 
14  because, “at the time the suit was filed” furlough contracts had been signed but no furlough 
15  days had been taken); Stanley v. University of Southern California, 13 F.3d 1313, 1320 (9th 
16  Cir. 1994) (preliminary injunction seeking to compel USC to install plaintiff as head coach was 
17  “mandatory” because on “the date th[e] action was filed in state court, Coach Stanley was no 
18  longer a USC employee” and her contract had expired).  Indeed, Plaintiff is challenging 
19  Defendants’ August 2018 withdrawal of $10,855,134.15 from Plaintiff’s account.  Thus, 
20  according to Plaintiff, the monies were taken before Plaintiff filed its Complaint in February 
21  2019.                                                                     
22       Because Plaintiff is seeking to compel Defendant to do something affirmative, the 
23  preliminary injunction is mandatory and must be considered under a stricter standard.  Plaintiff 
24  must demonstrate that the “facts and law clearly favor” a preliminary injunction. Id. 
25  ///                                                                       
1       B.   Winter test is not met                                          
2       Plaintiff first argues that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its Arizona common law 
3  fraud and constructive fraud claims. (Mot. at 4–9).  However, the Court will begin by 
4  addressing the element of irreparable harm.  Indeed, the basis of injunctive relief in the federal 
5  courts is irreparable harm and inadequacy of legal remedies. Sampson v. Murray, 415 U.S. 61, 
6  88 (1974).  “Purely economic harms are generally not irreparable, as money lost may be 
7  recovered later, in the ordinary course of litigation.” Idaho v. Coeur d’Alene Tribe, 794 F.3d 
8  1039, 1046 (9th Cir. 2015) (citing Sampson, 415 U.S. at 61–62).  “[A] preliminary injunction 
9  usually will be denied if it appears that the applicant has an adequate alternate remedy in the 
10  form of money damages or other relief.” 11A Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal 
11  Practice and Procedure § 2948.1 (3d ed. 2019).                            
12       Here, the harm Plaintiff asserts—the wrongful taking of $10,855,134.15 from its bank 
13  account—can be adequately addressed with legal remedies in the form of money damages.  To 
14  be sure, Plaintiff does maintain that it has suffered, or is likely to suffer, other harms.  For 
15  example, Plaintiff submits that “the harm [it will suffer] involves damage to reputational 
16  interests of a hospital serving an indigent population located on an Indian reservation where 
17  residents are often distrustful of outsiders given the unfortunate history in this country 
18  involving native populations.” (Mot. at 10).  However, Plaintiff cites no legal authority 
19  suggesting that this type of harm warrants a preliminary injunction under the relevant legal 
20  standard.  Moreover, Plaintiff notes that “the money taken by Defendants was, and continues to 
21  be, needed to provide ongoing medical care for the indigent population served by the hospital.” 
22  (Id.).  But even if the Court granted the requested relief, it would not alleviate the hospital’s 
23  financial needs, as the $10,855,134.15 would be placed in a third-party account pending the 
24  adjudication of this case.                                                
25                                                                            
1       Lastly, Plaintiff maintains that Defendants have placed Sage Memorial under the 
2  scrutiny of federal and Navajo authorities. (Id. at 11).  Plaintiffs rely on the Complaint’s 
3  allegations which provide that in a prior settlement with the United States, the United States 
4  agreed to pay the hospital $122,500,000.00. (Compl. ¶ 36).  Further,      
5       the  settlement  agreement . . . expressly  prohibited  the  hospital  from  providing 
        payment  to  any  management  company  or  affiliated  entity.    Notably,  the 
6       agreement  also  singled  out  Razaghi  by  name  by  further  providing  that  “[i]f 
        Ahmad R. Razaghi or any current officer or officer-level employee of a Razaghi-
7                                                                            
        related entity is convicted of a felony crime of fraud related to the management of 
8       [the] [h]ospital or any federal health care program operated by [the Hospital] 
        within 5 years of the effective date of this Settlement Agreement, [the Indian 
9       Health Service] may conduct additional monitoring on the expenditure of the 
        Settlement sum . . . .”  This provision clearly evinced the federal government’s 
10                                                                            
        concerns regarding Razaghi’s potential for fraudulent conduct.       
11                                                                            
12  (Id.).  But those allegations do not demonstrate that the federal or Navajo authorities have 
13  placed Plaintiff under additional scrutiny as a result of the conduct challenged in the instant 
14  case.  And Plaintiffs do not allege that Defendant Razaghi or any “officer-level employee of a 
15  Razaghi-related entity” has been convicted of a felony crime of fraud related to the 
16  management of the hospital or any federal health care program operated by the hospital, 
17  thereby subjecting Plaintiff to additional monitoring from the Indian Health Service (as per the 
18  settlement agreement).  More importantly, even assuming Plaintiff asserted these additional 
19  facts, Plaintiff nevertheless has not explained how the requested relief would address the 
20  purported harm.                                                           
21       In sum, Plaintiff has not demonstrated that it is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the 
22  absence of preliminary relief.  This is especially true in light of the very high burden for a 
23  mandatory preliminary injunction.  Because Plaintiff has failed to satisfy the necessary 
24  irreparable harm prong of the Winter test, the Court need not engage in additional analysis of 
25  the remaining elements.  Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction is denied.  
1  IV.  CONCLUSION                                                           
2       IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, (ECF 
3  No. 18), is DENIED.                                                       
4       IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that in light of the above, Defendants’ Motion to Stay 
5  Briefing and Consideration of Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, (ECF No. 22), or 
6  in the alternative, a Motion for Extension of Time to File Response, (ECF No. 23), are 
7  DENIED as moot.

24  “that he is likely to succeed on the merits,” (2) “that he is likely to suffer irreparable harm in 
25  the absence of preliminary relief,” (3) “that the balance of equities tips in his favor,” and (4) 
1  “that an injunction is in the public interest.” Id. at 20.  “[C]ourts must balance the competing 
2  claims of injury and must consider the effect on each party of the granting or withholding of the 
3  requested relief.” Id. at 24 (internal quotation marks omitted).          
4        The Ninth Circuit has held that “serious questions going to the merits and a hardship 
5  balance that tips sharply toward the plaintiff can support issuance of an injunction, assuming 
6  the other two elements of the Winter test are also met.” Alliance for the Wild Rockies v. 
7  Cottrell,
632 F.3d 1127, 1132
 (9th Cir. 2011) (internal quotation marks omitted). 
8  III.  DISCUSSION                                                          
9       Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction seeks what it characterizes as “two very 
10  simple things”: (1) a hearing to ascertain the location of the $10,855,134.15 allegedly taken by 
11  Defendants, and (2) an order directing those funds be placed into a trust account maintained by 
12  a third-party custodian pending the adjudication of this case. (Pl.’s Mot. Prelim. Inj. (“Mot”) at 
13  2, ECF No. 18).  In order to determine whether this “extraordinary remedy” is warranted, 
14  Winter,
555 U.S. at 22
, the Court will first address whether Plaintiff’s requested injunction is 
15  prohibitory or mandatory.  The Court will then consider whether Plaintiff has established the 
16  requisite preliminary injunction elements under Winter.                   
17       A.   Plaintiff requests a mandatory preliminary injunction           
18       A preliminary injunction may be either prohibitory or mandatory.  “A prohibitory 
19  injunction prohibits a party from taking action and preserves the status quo pending a 
20  determination of the action on the merits.” Marlyn Nutraceuticals, Inc. v. Mucos Pharma 
21  GmbH & Co.,
571 F.3d 873, 878
 (9th Cir. 2009) (internal quotations and alterations omitted).  
22  The status quo means “the last, uncontested status which preceded the pending controversy.” 
23  Regents of the Univ. of Cal. v. Am. Broad. Cos.,
747 F.2d 511
, 514 (9th Cir. 1984).  
24       In contrast, a mandatory injunction “orders a responsible party to ‘take action’” Meghrig 
25  v. KFC W., Inc.,
516 U.S. 479, 484
 (1996).  Mandatory injunctions are disfavored and “are not 
1  granted unless extreme or very serious damage will result.” Anderson v. United States, 612
2 F.2d 1112
, 1115 (9th Cir. 1980).  They “are not issued in doubtful cases or where the injury 
3  complained of is capable of compensation in damages.”
Id.
                 
4       Here, Plaintiff’s requested injunction is mandatory because it seeks to compel 
5  Defendants to do something they are not currently doing; that is, deposit funds into a third-
6  party trust account.  Insofar as Plaintiff represents that granting the injunction would return 
7  Plaintiff to the status quo prior to Defendants’ allegedly wrongful taking of $10.8 million, 
8  Plaintiff is mistaken. (Mot. at 11).  The status quo means “the last, uncontested status which 
9  preceded the pending controversy.’” Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 747 F.2d at 514.  And the 
10  “last uncontested status” is not measured from the time at which the first dispute at issue in a 
11  case arose, but from the time the complaint was filed. See N.D. ex rel. parents acting as 
12  guardians ad litem v. Hawaii Dep’t of Educ.,
600 F.3d 1104
, 1112 n.6 (9th Cir. 2010) 
13  (preliminary injunction prohibiting enforcement of new furlough policy was “prohibitory” 
14  because, “at the time the suit was filed” furlough contracts had been signed but no furlough 
15  days had been taken); Stanley v. University of Southern California,
13 F.3d 1313, 1320
 (9th 
16  Cir. 1994) (preliminary injunction seeking to compel USC to install plaintiff as head coach was 
17  “mandatory” because on “the date th[e] action was filed in state court, Coach Stanley was no 
18  longer a USC employee” and her contract had expired).  Indeed, Plaintiff is challenging 
19  Defendants’ August 2018 withdrawal of $10,855,134.15 from Plaintiff’s account.  Thus, 
20  according to Plaintiff, the monies were taken before Plaintiff filed its Complaint in February 
21  2019.                                                                     
22       Because Plaintiff is seeking to compel Defendant to do something affirmative, the 
23  preliminary injunction is mandatory and must be considered under a stricter standard.  Plaintiff 
24  must demonstrate that the “facts and law clearly favor” a preliminary injunction.
Id.
 
25  ///                                                                       
1       B.   Winter test is not met                                          
2       Plaintiff first argues that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its Arizona common law 
3  fraud and constructive fraud claims. (Mot. at 4–9).  However, the Court will begin by 
4  addressing the element of irreparable harm.  Indeed, the basis of injunctive relief in the federal 
5  courts is irreparable harm and inadequacy of legal remedies. Sampson v. Murray,
415 U.S. 61
, 
6  88 (1974).  “Purely economic harms are generally not irreparable, as money lost may be 
7  recovered later, in the ordinary course of litigation.” Idaho v. Coeur d’Alene Tribe,
794 F.3d 8 1039, 1046
 (9th Cir. 2015) (citing Sampson, 415 U.S. at 61–62).  “[A] preliminary injunction 
9  usually will be denied if it appears that the applicant has an adequate alternate remedy in the 
10  form of money damages or other relief.” 11A Charles Alan Wright & Arthur R. Miller, Federal 
11  Practice and Procedure § 2948.1 (3d ed. 2019).                            
12       Here, the harm Plaintiff asserts—the wrongful taking of $10,855,134.15 from its bank 
13  account—can be adequately addressed with legal remedies in the form of money damages.  To 
14  be sure, Plaintiff does maintain that it has suffered, or is likely to suffer, other harms.  For 
15  example, Plaintiff submits that “the harm [it will suffer] involves damage to reputational 
16  interests of a hospital serving an indigent population located on an Indian reservation where 
17  residents are often distrustful of outsiders given the unfortunate history in this country 
18  involving native populations.” (Mot. at 10).  However, Plaintiff cites no legal authority 
19  suggesting that this type of harm warrants a preliminary injunction under the relevant legal 
20  standard.  Moreover, Plaintiff notes that “the money taken by Defendants was, and continues to 
21  be, needed to provide ongoing medical care for the indigent population served by the hospital.” 
22  (Id.).  But even if the Court granted the requested relief, it would not alleviate the hospital’s 
23  financial needs, as the $10,855,134.15 would be placed in a third-party account pending the 
24  adjudication of this case.                                                
25                                                                            
1       Lastly, Plaintiff maintains that Defendants have placed Sage Memorial under the 
2  scrutiny of federal and Navajo authorities. (Id. at 11).  Plaintiffs rely on the Complaint’s 
3  allegations which provide that in a prior settlement with the United States, the United States 
4  agreed to pay the hospital $122,500,000.00. (Compl. ¶ 36).  Further,      
5       the  settlement  agreement . . . expressly  prohibited  the  hospital  from  providing 
        payment  to  any  management  company  or  affiliated  entity.    Notably,  the 
6       agreement  also  singled  out  Razaghi  by  name  by  further  providing  that  “[i]f 
        Ahmad R. Razaghi or any current officer or officer-level employee of a Razaghi-
7                                                                            
        related entity is convicted of a felony crime of fraud related to the management of 
8       [the] [h]ospital or any federal health care program operated by [the Hospital] 
        within 5 years of the effective date of this Settlement Agreement, [the Indian 
9       Health Service] may conduct additional monitoring on the expenditure of the 
        Settlement sum . . . .”  This provision clearly evinced the federal government’s 
10                                                                            
        concerns regarding Razaghi’s potential for fraudulent conduct.       
11                                                                            
12  (Id.).  But those allegations do not demonstrate that the federal or Navajo authorities have 
13  placed Plaintiff under additional scrutiny as a result of the conduct challenged in the instant 
14  case.  And Plaintiffs do not allege that Defendant Razaghi or any “officer-level employee of a 
15  Razaghi-related entity” has been convicted of a felony crime of fraud related to the 
16  management of the hospital or any federal health care program operated by the hospital, 
17  thereby subjecting Plaintiff to additional monitoring from the Indian Health Service (as per the 
18  settlement agreement).  More importantly, even assuming Plaintiff asserted these additional 
19  facts, Plaintiff nevertheless has not explained how the requested relief would address the 
20  purported harm.                                                           
21       In sum, Plaintiff has not demonstrated that it is likely to suffer irreparable harm in the 
22  absence of preliminary relief.  This is especially true in light of the very high burden for a 
23  mandatory preliminary injunction.  Because Plaintiff has failed to satisfy the necessary 
24  irreparable harm prong of the Winter test, the Court need not engage in additional analysis of 
25  the remaining elements.  Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction is denied.  
1  IV.  CONCLUSION                                                           
2       IT IS HEREBY ORDERED that Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, (ECF 
3  No. 18), is DENIED.                                                       
4       IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that in light of the above, Defendants’ Motion to Stay 
5  Briefing and Consideration of Plaintiff’s Motion for Preliminary Injunction, (ECF No. 22), or 
6  in the alternative, a Motion for Extension of Time to File Response, (ECF No. 23), are 
7  DENIED as moot.

19      This case arises from Defendants’ alleged scheme to defraud Sage of over $10.8 million 
20  through Defendants’ deceptive acquisition and invocation of a lucrative termination payment

24  Nation community in rural Ganado, Arizona. (Id. ¶ 23).  The majority of Sage’s operation 
25  budget comes from the Indian Health Service (“IHS”), an agency within the U.S. Department 
1  of Health and Human Services. (Id. ¶ 24).  Principally, Sage alleges that Defendants 
2  fraudulently induced Sage’s Board of Directors (“BOD”) to unwittingly authorize a contractual 
3  amendment to the parties’ Management Services Contract containing an extremely generous 
4  termination payment, which Defendants invoked to siphon $10.8 million from Sage’s operating 
5  budget. (See id. ¶¶ 39–57).  The Court’s below discussion provides background on the 
6  relationship between Sage and Defendants, up to and including the scheme described in the 
7  Complaint.                                                                
8       A.   SAGE ENGAGES RAZAGHI TO MANAGE HOSPITAL OPERATIONS              
9       Pursuant to Sage’s bylaws, every member of its BOD must be a member of the Navajo 
10  Nation and reside in the community in or around Ganado, Arizona. (Id. ¶ 21).  Sometime in 
11  2007, “Razaghi and his brother partnered with a friend, Manuel Morgan (‘Morgan’), a member 
12  of the Navajo Tribe and former Navajo Nation County Commissioner, to form Morgan & 
13  Associates, LLC, a company in which Morgan [held] majority ownership so that the entity 
14  could qualify as a Navajo business.” (Id. ¶ 26).  Sage alleges that Razaghi, leveraging Morgan’s 
15  status as a member of the Navajo Nation, persuaded Sage to award Morgan & Associates a 
16  management services contract. (Id. ¶ 27).  Under the terms of this contract, Razaghi would 
17  serve as Sage’s “Contract CEO.” (Id.).  Sage claims Razaghi subsequently created business 
18  entities, including RDC, to supply Sage with medical personnel at a profit. (Id. ¶ 28). 
19      On March 18, 2011, RDC1 entered into the Management Services Contract with Sage’s 
20  BOD. (Id. ¶ 29).  This contract replaced Morgan & Associates’ contract with the hospital and 
21  placed management of Sage under Razaghi and RDC’s control. (Id.).  Sage alleges that this was 
22  when the “multiple different schemes to defraud Sage Memorial began through the use of the 

23  mail and interstate wires.” (Id.).                                       
24                                                                           

25                                                                           
1 The Court’s use of “RDC” is inclusive of allegations concerning predecessor entities such as “Razaghi

5  States agreed to pay $122,500,000.00 to settle the litigation with Sage.  Sage represents that 
6  the:

14      D.   THE SECOND AMENDMENT TO THE MANAGEMENT SERVICES

3  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
4       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) mandates that a court dismiss a cause of action 
5  that fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. See N. Star Int’l v. Ariz. Corp. 
6  Comm’n, 720 F.2d 578, 581 (9th Cir. 1983).  When considering a motion to dismiss under Rule 
7  12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, dismissal is appropriate only when the complaint does not 
8  give the defendant fair notice of a legally cognizable claim and the grounds on which it rests. 
9  See Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007).  In considering whether the 
10  complaint is sufficient to state a claim, the Court will take all material allegations as true and 
11  construe them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. See NL Indus., Inc. v. Kaplan, 792 
12  F.2d 896, 898 (9th Cir. 1986).                                           
13      The Court, however, is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely 
14  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences. See Sprewell v. Golden 
15  State Warriors, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir. 2001).  A formulaic recitation of a cause of action 
16  with conclusory allegations is not sufficient; a plaintiff must plead facts showing that a 
17  violation is plausible, not just possible. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (citing 
18  Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555).                                               
19      A court may also dismiss a complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) 
20  for failure to comply with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a). Hearns v. San Bernardino 
21  Police Dept., 530 F.3d 1124, 1129 (9th Cir. 2008).  Rule 8(a)(2) requires that a plaintiff’s 
22  complaint contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled 

23  to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2).  Furthermore, the Supreme Court has rejected any sort of 
24  “heightened” pleading requirement for § 1983 municipal liability claims because such a 
25  heightened pleading standard cannot be “square[d] . . . with the liberal system of ‘notice 
1  pleading’ set up by the Federal Rules.” Leatherman v. Tarrant Cty. Narcotics Intelligence & 
2  Coordination Unit, 507 U.S. 163, 164 (1993).                              
3       “Generally, a district court may not consider any material beyond the pleadings in ruling 
4  on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion . . . . However, material which is properly submitted as part of the 
5  complaint may be considered on a motion to dismiss.” Hal Roach Studios, Inc. v. Richard 
6  Feiner & Co., 896 F.2d 1542, 1555 n.19 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).  Similarly, 
7  “documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party 
8  questions, but which are not physically attached to the pleading, may be considered in ruling on 
9  a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss” without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for 
10  summary judgment. Branch v. Tunnell, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994).  Under Federal Rule 
11  of Evidence 201, a court may take judicial notice of “matters of public record.” Mack v. S. Bay 
12  Beer Distrib., 798 F.2d 1279, 1282 (9th Cir. 1986).  Otherwise, if the district court considers 
13  materials outside of the pleadings, the motion to dismiss becomes a motion for summary 
14  judgment. See Arpin v. Santa Clara Valley Transp. Agency, 261 F.3d 912, 925 (9th Cir. 2001). 
15      Additionally, “[i]n alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity the 
16  circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).  The rule requires that claims 
17  of fraud be accompanied by the “who, what, when, where, and how” of the conduct charged, 
18  Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp., USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1106 (9th Cir. 2003) (quoting Cooper v. 
19  Pickett, 137 F.3d 616, 627 (9th Cir. 1997)), so that the complaint may not simply “lump 
20  multiple defendants together.” Destfino v. Reiswig, 630 F.3d 952, 958 (9th Cir. 2011).  In other 
21  words, the complaint “must include ‘an account of the time, place, and specific content of the 
22  false representations as well as the identities of the parties to the misrepresentations.’” Depot, 

23  Inc. v. Caring for Montanans, Inc., 915 F.3d 643, 668 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Swartz v. 
24  KPMG, LLP, 476 F.3d 756, 764 (9th Cir. 2007) (per curiam)) (internal quotations omitted).  
25  Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement ensures that the defendants are on “notice of the particular 
1  misconduct . . . so that they can defend against the charge and not just deny that they have done 
2  anything wrong.” Vess, 317 F.3d at 1106 (internal quotations omitted).    
3       If the court grants a motion to dismiss, it must then decide whether to grant leave to 
4  amend.  The court should “freely give” leave to amend when there is no “undue delay, bad 
5  faith[,] dilatory motive on the part of the movant . . . undue prejudice to the opposing party by 
6  virtue of . . . the amendment, [or] futility of the amendment . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a); Foman 
7  v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962).  Generally, leave to amend is only denied when it is clear 
8  that the deficiencies of the complaint cannot be cured by amendment. See DeSoto v. Yellow 
9  Freight Sys., Inc., 957 F.2d 655, 658 (9th Cir. 1992).

3  II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                       
4       Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) mandates that a court dismiss a cause of action 
5  that fails to state a claim upon which relief can be granted. See N. Star Int’l v. Ariz. Corp. 
6  Comm’n,
720 F.2d 578, 581
 (9th Cir. 1983).  When considering a motion to dismiss under Rule 
7  12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, dismissal is appropriate only when the complaint does not 
8  give the defendant fair notice of a legally cognizable claim and the grounds on which it rests. 
9  See Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly,
550 U.S. 544, 555
 (2007).  In considering whether the 
10  complaint is sufficient to state a claim, the Court will take all material allegations as true and 
11  construe them in the light most favorable to the plaintiff. See NL Indus., Inc. v. Kaplan, 792
12 F.2d 896, 898
 (9th Cir. 1986).                                           
13      The Court, however, is not required to accept as true allegations that are merely 
14  conclusory, unwarranted deductions of fact, or unreasonable inferences. See Sprewell v. Golden 
15  State Warriors,
266 F.3d 979, 988
 (9th Cir. 2001).  A formulaic recitation of a cause of action 
16  with conclusory allegations is not sufficient; a plaintiff must plead facts showing that a 
17  violation is plausible, not just possible. Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (citing 
18  Twombly,
550 U.S. at 555
).                                               
19      A court may also dismiss a complaint pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) 
20  for failure to comply with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a). Hearns v. San Bernardino 
21  Police Dept.,
530 F.3d 1124, 1129
 (9th Cir. 2008).  Rule 8(a)(2) requires that a plaintiff’s 
22  complaint contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled 

23  to relief.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2).  Furthermore, the Supreme Court has rejected any sort of 
24  “heightened” pleading requirement for § 1983 municipal liability claims because such a 
25  heightened pleading standard cannot be “square[d] . . . with the liberal system of ‘notice 
1  pleading’ set up by the Federal Rules.” Leatherman v. Tarrant Cty. Narcotics Intelligence & 
2  Coordination Unit,
507 U.S. 163, 164
 (1993).                              
3       “Generally, a district court may not consider any material beyond the pleadings in ruling 
4  on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion . . . . However, material which is properly submitted as part of the 
5  complaint may be considered on a motion to dismiss.” Hal Roach Studios, Inc. v. Richard 
6  Feiner & Co.,
896 F.2d 1542
, 1555 n.19 (9th Cir. 1990) (citations omitted).  Similarly, 
7  “documents whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party 
8  questions, but which are not physically attached to the pleading, may be considered in ruling on 
9  a Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss” without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for 
10  summary judgment. Branch v. Tunnell,
14 F.3d 449, 454
 (9th Cir. 1994).  Under Federal Rule 
11  of Evidence 201, a court may take judicial notice of “matters of public record.” Mack v. S. Bay 
12  Beer Distrib.,
798 F.2d 1279, 1282
 (9th Cir. 1986).  Otherwise, if the district court considers 
13  materials outside of the pleadings, the motion to dismiss becomes a motion for summary 
14  judgment. See Arpin v. Santa Clara Valley Transp. Agency,
261 F.3d 912
, 925 (9th Cir. 2001). 
15      Additionally, “[i]n alleging fraud or mistake, a party must state with particularity the 
16  circumstances constituting fraud or mistake.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b).  The rule requires that claims 
17  of fraud be accompanied by the “who, what, when, where, and how” of the conduct charged, 
18  Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp., USA,
317 F.3d 1097, 1106
 (9th Cir. 2003) (quoting Cooper v. 
19  Pickett,
137 F.3d 616, 627
 (9th Cir. 1997)), so that the complaint may not simply “lump 
20  multiple defendants together.” Destfino v. Reiswig,
630 F.3d 952, 958
 (9th Cir. 2011).  In other 
21  words, the complaint “must include ‘an account of the time, place, and specific content of the 
22  false representations as well as the identities of the parties to the misrepresentations.’” Depot, 

23  Inc. v. Caring for Montanans, Inc.,
915 F.3d 643, 668
 (9th Cir. 2019) (quoting Swartz v. 
24  KPMG, LLP,
476 F.3d 756, 764
 (9th Cir. 2007) (per curiam)) (internal quotations omitted).  
25  Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement ensures that the defendants are on “notice of the particular 
1  misconduct . . . so that they can defend against the charge and not just deny that they have done 
2  anything wrong.” Vess,
317 F.3d at 1106
 (internal quotations omitted).    
3       If the court grants a motion to dismiss, it must then decide whether to grant leave to 
4  amend.  The court should “freely give” leave to amend when there is no “undue delay, bad 
5  faith[,] dilatory motive on the part of the movant . . . undue prejudice to the opposing party by 
6  virtue of . . . the amendment, [or] futility of the amendment . . . .” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a); Foman 
7  v. Davis,
371 U.S. 178, 182
 (1962).  Generally, leave to amend is only denied when it is clear 
8  that the deficiencies of the complaint cannot be cured by amendment. See DeSoto v. Yellow 
9  Freight Sys., Inc.,
957 F.2d 655, 658
 (9th Cir. 1992).

18 U.S.C. §§ 1341
